title: Desire, gently
hook: for now, don't desire what isn't up to you; only choose and refuse lightly (Enchiridion 2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: George Long's translation and the two piles, what is ours and what isn't. Your line was start here.

Every want comes with a promise tucked inside it. Want the job, and the want quietly promises: you'll get it. Dread the diagnosis, and the dread promises: you'll escape it. The promise is easy to miss until it breaks, and then the disappointment can seem like something done to us. Section two of the handbook takes those promises seriously. It doesn't tell a beginner to stop wanting forever. It says something gentler, and odder, with two small words that matter a lot: for now.
screen: `EVERY WANT HIDES A PROMISE.` → `THE PROMISE BREAKS.` → `FOR NOW.`

segments.voice: Desire, Epictetus says, promises that you'll get what you desire; aversion promises that you won't fall into what you avoid. Miss what you desire and you feel unlucky. Fall into what you avoid and you feel wretched. So move aversion home. If you only push away things in your own power, like your own cruelty or cowardice, you'll never fall into them against your will. Try to avoid sickness, death or poverty, and you've signed up for misery, because those aren't yours to avoid. So he says: take aversion off everything outside your power, and set it on the things inside it. Then the surprise. For the present, he says, set desire aside completely. Desire what isn't up to you and you're bound to be disappointed, and the good things that are up to you, a steady character, sound judgment, aren't yet within a beginner's reach. This is advice for someone starting out, not a rule for a whole life. Meanwhile, use only choosing and refusing, moving toward a thing or away from it, and do even that lightly, without straining, with a reservation. The Stoics meant a quiet clause attached to a plan. Seneca gives one: I'll sail, unless something gets in the way. Neighbors say something close. Muslims say in sha Allah, if God wills, and the letter of James in the New Testament says to speak of plans with: if the Lord will. Epictetus' version is simply: lightly, and for now.
screen: `DESIRE AND AVERSION MAKE PROMISES.` · `AVOID ONLY WHAT IS YOURS TO AVOID.` · `FOR NOW, SET DESIRE DOWN.` · `CHOOSE LIGHTLY, WITH A RESERVATION.` · then, large: `GENTLY, FOR NOW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you want that isn't fully up to you, a reply, a result, a yes from someone, and feel where the want pulls in your body. Without pushing it away, add the quiet clause inside: I'd like this, if nothing prevents it. You're still allowed to want it; you're just holding it in an open hand.
Desire. In the handbook, a want that promises to get. For a beginner, Epictetus says: set it down for now, and choose lightly instead. Today's word.
Your line: gently, for now. A plan can carry a quiet unless and still be a real plan. That's day three hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners add a quiet reservation to their plans, such as 'if nothing prevents me', so they can act fully while holding the outcome lightly.

chat.says: Do Stoics really say you should never want anything?
options: No, the handbook tells beginners to set desire aside for now and choose lightly.
Yes, Epictetus says to give up every desire for the rest of your life.
No, it says want things hard and push until you get them.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): 'disappointment is likely' changed to 'bound to be disappointed' to match the text's necessity; 'a clause attached to every plan' (absolute, and the market example is not in Enchiridion 2) replaced by Seneca's sailing example, now cited; Discourses 3.2 added to sources for the trapdoor; a generalization about the listener softened.

Enchiridion 2 paraphrased throughout (desire and aversion's promises; move aversion to things in our power; take away desire 'for the present'; use only choosing and refusing, lightly, with reservation).

The market example of a reservation is a standard illustration in modern discussions (Seneca, On Tranquility 13, uses a similar formula); it is not in Enchiridion 2 itself. Confirm phrasing 'The Stoics meant…'.
Greek ὄρεξις, and hupexairesis (ὑπεξαίρεσις) as the term behind 'with reservation': confirm.
Epictetus' three fields of study (desire/aversion, impulse/duty, assent) are set out in Discourses 3.2; confirm the trapdoor wording.
Neighbors (in sha Allah; James 4:15) mentioned briefly and without comparison.
